title: Systemic lupus erythematosus with acute ischemic optic neuropathy complicated with neuromyelitis optica: a case report
case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Bangladeshi woman with a 2-month history of polyarthralgia, photosensitive rash, intermittent fever, oral ulcers, and alopecia presented with sudden, progressive, painless vision loss in both eyes and progressive weakness of both lower limbs over 48 hours. She denied headaches, seizures, bowel or bladder dysfunction, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or trauma. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. She had a malar rash, oral ulceration, alopecia, and swollen tender wrist joints. Visual acuity was reduced to hand movements bilaterally; light projection was intact, the direct pupillary reflex was sluggish, and the consensual reflex was normal. Intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg in both eyes. Fundoscopy showed bilateral pale, swollen optic discs with a superotemporal flame-shaped hemorrhage in the right optic disc. 

Neurologic examination revealed bilateral upper motor neuron–type weakness in the lower limbs (muscle power reduced with brisk knee and ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses) and sensory loss to pain, temperature, and joint position up to the T8 level. Other systemic findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, strongly positive ANA (homogeneous), high-titer anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, low complement levels (C3, C4), and positive anti–aquaporin-4 IgG antibody. Cerebrospinal fluid was normal, with absent oligoclonal bands. 

MRI of the spine with contrast revealed multiple enhancing T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the cervical and dorsal cord extending over more than three vertebral segments with diffuse cord edema; MRI of the brain and orbits was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of SLE-associated ischemic optic neuropathy — “Our patient presented with bilateral acute painless loss of vision with optic disc swelling that was in favor of ischemic optic neuropathy related to SLE-induced vasculitis.”  
2. Consideration of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder — “the presence of highly specific anti-NMO IgG antibodies in high titer along with the longitudinally extensive lesions in both cervical and dorsal spinal cord.”  
3. Consideration of relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis — “A typical MRI pattern of multiple sclerosis is at least one lesion on a T2-weighted scan … In the spinal cord, the lesion will be a short segment. On the contrary, the presence of anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies with longitudinally extensive lesions in the spinal cord … goes more in favor of NMOSD.”  
4. Consideration of SLE-associated transverse myelitis — “it is very unlikely that SLE causes longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion and anti-NMO antibody.”
